posts.title: npm supply chain attack and anthropic code leak
posts.summary: Feeling better about the future of software jobs after seeing two crazy incidents in one day.
posts.content: Today npm experienced a supply chain attack and Anthropic had their source code leaked. Axios, an HTTP libary that comes with Node.js with over 100 million weekly downloads, was compromised in the attack. Anthropic had their source code leaked via a .map file, intended for internal debugging only, being included in their latest version of their package on the public npm registry. I've been feeling pretty miserable about the future of the software industry recently but this made me smile a little bit. There are still accidents happening all over the tech world, with even the biggest companies involved, and software engineers may still have a role to play.

posts.title: PSU Test Complaint
posts.summary: Best Buy tried to charge me $100 for a PSU test
posts.content: My PC stopped working in late January and I diagnosed it as a power supply failure pretty quickly. Today I tested it with a multimeter and a paperclip and determined it was almost definitely the issue, but I wanted an expert opinion. Drove over to Best Buy where the guy looked like he had never seen a power supply before. He talked to his manager and determined they would charge me $100 to test it. I left the store immediately and went over to uBreakiFix. They tested it right away and for completely free and it only took about 2 minutes. Very surprised to find out today just how clueless some Geek Squad employees just might be.

posts.title: Building a RAG Chatbot for an Online Course
posts.summary: A behind-the-scenes look at building an AI-powered course assistant using LangChain and FAISS.
posts.content:
My current senior project is an AI chatbot embedded into a Thinkific-based leadership training course. The idea is that learners can ask the chatbot questions, and it responds using the actual course material rather than just hallucinating answers.

The core of it is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. We process all the course PDFs and text into vector embeddings using LangChain, store them in a FAISS index, and then, at query time, we retrieve the most relevant chunks and pass them to an LLM as context.

The trickiest part so far has been chunking strategy: too small and you lose context, too large and you waste the context window. We ended up with overlapping chunks of ~500 tokens which seems to strike a good balance.

The frontend is a lightweight chat widget built in plain HTML/CSS/JS that floats over the course content. More updates to come as this progresses!
